lessons.title: For Loops
lessons.introduction: A for loop repeats a block of code a known, counted number of times — ideal for blinking N times, sweeping a servo, or iterating arrays.
objectives: Write a for loop with initializer, condition, and step update.
Trace loop counter values from start to finish.
Use a for loop to sweep PWM brightness smoothly.
conceptExplanation: Whenever you know how many times an action should repeat — like flashing an LED 5 times or stepping a servo from 0 to 180 degrees — a for loop keeps all three loop controls cleanly in one header.
lessons.analogy: A for loop is like doing 10 push-ups: start at 1, keep going while count <= 10, add 1 after each rep.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for For Loops:
rules: Three parts separated by semicolons: start; condition; update.
Avoid off-by-one errors: i < 5 runs 5 times (0..4); i <= 5 runs 6 times (0..5).

codeExamples.title: Smooth LED Fade with a For Loop
codeExamples.description: Ramps PWM brightness on pin 9 from 0 to 255.

lineByLine.explanation: Continues while brightness is at most 255.
Increases brightness in steps of 5 each pass.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Servo sweeps, LED strip animations, and taking 10 sensor samples to average noise all rely on for loops.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using <= when iterating an array of length N
commonMistakes.fix: Array indices end at N-1, so use i < N.

commonMistakes.mistake: Creating an infinite loop with the wrong update direction
commonMistakes.fix: If counting down from 10 to 0, use i-- not i++.

tryItYourself.title: m05_for_loop.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a second for loop that fades brightness back down from 255 to 0.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Pin 9 smoothly breathes from dark to full brightness and back down.

exercises.prompt: How many times does this loop print?
exercises.explanation: Starting at 0 while i < 4 runs for i = 0, 1, 2, and 3 (4 times total).

exercises.prompt: Complete the for loop to count from 1 to 5 inclusive.

summary: for loops bundle initialization, condition, and step into one header.
Great for counted repetitions, PWM fades, and sensor sampling.
Watch out for off-by-one (< vs <=) boundaries.

lessons.title: While Loops
lessons.introduction: A while loop repeats as long as a condition remains true — ideal when you don't know in advance how many repetitions it will take.
objectives: Prevent accidental infinite loops by updating the condition inside the loop.
Wait for a button release or calibration trigger safely.
conceptExplanation: Unlike a for loop with a fixed count, a while loop keeps checking a condition before every pass. If the condition is false at the start, the body runs zero times.
lessons.analogy: Think of filling a water tank: WHILE the tank is not full, keep the valve open.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for While Loops:
rules: Something inside the loop (or a hardware input) MUST eventually make the condition false.
On ESP32, long blocking while loops without delay() can trigger the Watchdog Timer!

codeExamples.title: Wait for Start Button
codeExamples.description: Pauses in setup() until the student presses the start button.

lineByLine.explanation: Stays waiting while button is unpressed (HIGH).
Small pause keeps CPU friendly (and feeds ESP32 watchdog).

lessons.realWorldApplication: Competition robots use a while loop in setup() to wait for the referee's start button before driving.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to update the loop variable
commonMistakes.fix: Always increment/change the tested variable inside the loop body.

tryItYourself.title: m05_while_loop.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change the wait loop to print a dot '.' every 500 ms while waiting.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints dots every half second until pin 2 connects to GND, then prints 'Started!'.

exercises.prompt: If a while loop's condition is false on the very first check, how many times does its body run?
exercises.explanation: while tests its condition BEFORE entering the body.

exercises.prompt: Why does this loop run forever?
options: n is never decremented inside the loop, so n > 0 stays true forever.
exercises.explanation: Add n--; inside the loop so n reaches 0 and exits.

summary: while loops repeat as long as a condition remains true.
A while loop may execute 0 times if initially false.
Always ensure the loop condition can become false.

lessons.title: Do-While Loops
lessons.introduction: A do-while loop runs its body at least once before checking the condition at the bottom.
objectives: Compare do-while with standard while loops.
Apply do-while when you must take at least one sensor reading before deciding to retry.
conceptExplanation: Because the condition sits at the end of a do-while loop, the statements inside { } are guaranteed to execute at least one time — even if the condition turns out to be false.
lessons.analogy: Sampling soup before seasoning: you taste it at least once, and keep adding a pinch WHILE it still tastes bland.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Do-While Loops:
rules: Notice the required semicolon ';' right after while (condition);!

codeExamples.title: Retry Until Valid Sensor Reading
codeExamples.description: Reads a sensor at least once and retries if reading is 0.

lineByLine.explanation: Guarantees analogRead(A0) runs at least once.
Retries up to 5 times if reading is 0, preventing infinite hangs.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Sensor initialization handshakes use do-while with a max-retry cap so the robot attempts connection at least once without freezing forever.

commonMistakes.fix: Unlike while, do-while requires a trailing semicolon.

tryItYourself.title: m05_do_while.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Increase the max retry limit from 5 to 10.

exercises.prompt: What is the key difference between while and do-while?
options: do-while always executes its body at least once before testing the condition.
while requires a semicolon at the end of its block.
exercises.explanation: do-while checks its condition at the bottom of the loop.

summary: do-while always executes at least once.
Always include the trailing semicolon after while (condition);.
Cap retries to prevent infinite loops on faulty hardware.

lessons.title: Nested Loops
lessons.introduction: A nested loop places one loop inside another to handle grids, LED matrices, or repeated pattern groups.
objectives: Trace outer and inner loop counters step by step.
Use nested loops for multi-burst alert patterns.
conceptExplanation: For every single iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all the way from start to finish. An outer loop of 3 with an inner loop of 4 executes the inner body 3 * 4 = 12 times.
lessons.analogy: Think of a clock: for every 1 hour step (outer loop), the minute hand completes 60 full steps (inner loop).

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Nested Loops:
rules: Always use distinct counter names (e.g., row and col, or i and j) so inner and outer counters don't collide.

codeExamples.title: 3-Burst SOS Blink Pattern
codeExamples.description: Outer loop repeats 3 bursts; inner loop blinks 3 quick pulses per burst.

lineByLine.explanation: Inner loop produces 3 blinks inside each group (9 blinks total).

lessons.realWorldApplication: Scanning 8x8 LED matrices (like on Arduino Uno R4 WiFi) or keypads uses nested row/column loops.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reusing 'i' for both outer and inner loops
commonMistakes.fix: Use descriptive names like row/col or burst/pulse.

tryItYourself.title: m05_nested_loops.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change the inner loop to 2 pulses per burst for 6 total blinks.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints coordinate pairs (0,0) through (1,2) in Serial Monitor.

exercises.prompt: How many total times does Serial.print('*') run?
exercises.explanation: 3 outer iterations x 5 inner iterations = 15 total executions.

summary: Nested loops run the full inner loop for each single step of the outer loop.
Use distinct counter variable names for each loop level.
Total inner runs = outer count * inner count.

lessons.title: Break and Continue
lessons.introduction: break exits a loop immediately, while continue skips the rest of the current pass and jumps to the next iteration.
objectives: Use break to abort a loop early on an emergency stop or target found.
Use continue to ignore bad or out-of-range sensor samples.
Trace exact output when break or continue runs.
conceptExplanation: Sometimes you don't want to finish all remaining loop iterations — for example, if an emergency stop button is pressed mid-sweep, break exits immediately. If one sensor reading is noisy (-1), continue skips that bad sample without stopping the whole loop.
lessons.analogy: break is pulling the emergency exit door to leave the train; continue is skipping one station and staying on board.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Break and Continue:
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
if (emergencyStop) break;      // Exit loop completely
if (sample < 0) continue;     // Skip this iteration only
rules: break exits only the innermost enclosing loop (or switch).
In a for loop, continue still executes the step update (i++).

codeExamples.title: Filtering Bad Samples & Emergency Abort
codeExamples.description: Skips negative samples with continue and stops early if value exceeds 900.

lineByLine.explanation: Prints abort message and exits before ever reaching 200.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Safety monitors inside motor ramp loops check an E-stop pin every step and call break immediately if triggered.

commonMistakes.fix: break leaves the entire loop; continue only skips to the next iteration.

tryItYourself.title: m05_break_continue.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change 950 to 500 in the array and trace what prints now.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: With 500 instead of 950, prints 120, 340, 500, and 200 (still skipping -1).

exercises.explanation: 3 is skipped by continue, and 5 exits before printing via break.

summary: continue skips the remainder of the current iteration and moves to the next.
Use break for emergency aborts and continue for filtering invalid samples.
